own_scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?

refs.para: Another 1990s hybridization is rapcore. Body Count, led by rapper Ice-T, addressed themes that had crossover appeal to young males of all races.³³> The use of rapped vocals became rather popular later in the decade, although few bands that used them could be called metal.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: El metal en los noventa

refs.q: Spin’s 1998 feature on “New Metal,” which focused on bands like Korn and Limp Bizkit, was not free of denigration either
refs.para: Spin’s 1998 feature on “New Metal,” which focused on bands like Korn and Limp Bizkit, was not free of denigration either: Their music offered “traditional metal ferocity minus the corny hail-Satanism, Tawny Kitean videos, and big hair of the ’80s. . . .”⁴⁰ “New Metal” is defined by Spin as “a forward-looking hybrid that takes as many cues from alternative rock, hip-hop, and SoCal hardcore skate culture as it does from Black Sabbath and Slayer. For instance, Limp Bizkit, with their rapped vocals and full-time DJ, are New Metal.”⁴¹ Recognizing the style’s myriad ancestors, why call it metal rather than hip-hop, alternative, or some other term that doesn’t mention any of its constituent genres? Why label it metal, when members of these bands have stated that they are not at all desirous to be tagged with that term?⁴² One answer is that calling it metal gives the hybrid a more familiar, and perhaps a more white and more rock, image. The promiscuous use of “metal” is itself a demonstration that metal is back, as well as a cause of that comeback.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: El metal en los noventa

podcast.title: Judgment Night Soundtrack as Catalyst (1993)
podcast.body: The 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack, featuring unprecedented collaborations between rock and hip-hop acts, served as a major catalyst for the creation of nu metal. This project, which brought together 11 diverse pairings, helped popularize the crossover of these genres and led to the widespread success of nu metal later in the 1990s. "In retrospect, this was a major catalyst for the creation of rap rock and new metal, two genres that would be very, very big later in the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence (Late 1995)
podcast.body: Nu Metal emerged after 1995 as Alt Rock fragmented, characterized as an "overly aggressive and not too bright fusion of heavy metal and hip hop." "This is where we encounter new metal, which in retrospect was an overly aggressive and not too bright fusion of heavy metal and hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Polarizing Nature (2000)
podcast.body: While successful in terms of sales (e.g., Limp Bizkit, Papa Roach), the "sound and the attitude of New Metal was just so polarizing that it could only go so far" in carrying rock music at the turn of the millennium. "But the sound and the attitude of New Metal was just so polarizing that it could only go so far."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Polarizing Genre in 2001
podcast.body: In the summer of 2001, new metal was the biggest thing in music, but it was also a "very, very polarizing" genre. Listeners typically had strong opinions, either being intensely interested in it or completely disliking it. "New metal, the biggest thing at the time, was very, very polarizing. You were either really into it or you hated it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Categorization Challenges
podcast.body: Some bands initially categorized as new metal, such as Incubus, Puddle of Mud, Evanescence, Orgy, Papa Roach, and 3Days Grace, were easily digestible and eventually "escaped that classification," which many fought hard to do. "Some were easily digestible. And maybe some of them should have never been categorized under the heading of new metal to begin with."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contribution to Industrial Hip Hop Momentum
podcast.body: Nu-metal bands are noted for helping Industrial Hip Hop gain momentum in the 1990s, by incorporating rap rock sounds. "Any number of new metal bands also helped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Critical Reception (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: In the early 2000s, new metal often faced critical dismissal, as evidenced by the "critical pasting" of Linkin Park's debut single "One Step Closer" for being perceived as "more of the same old new metal." "it got a critical pasting because it was, well, more of the same old and new metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: At the start of the new century, the music scene began to move away from Nu Metal. "At the start of the new century, we began to move away from electronica new metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline and Linkin Park's Accessibility
podcast.body: By the early 2000s, the "whole new metal thing was largely over," but Linkin Park continued to achieve significant success. This was attributed to their sound being notably more "accessible" and "super radio friendly" than other bands within the genre. "And even though the whole new metal thing was largely over, Lincoln Park didn't care. But then again, no one from that whole genre sounded as accessible as them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline by Mid-2000s
podcast.body: By the mid-2000s, the "new metal" genre was considered "dead," leading bands like Linkin Park to intentionally reduce their rap elements in later albums due to uncertainty about fan acceptance. "The new metal was dead so the amount of wrapping that fans might find acceptable was uncertain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition and Sound
podcast.body: New metal incorporated elements of grunge and traditional metal, frequently featuring rap-like vocals. Its sound was characterized as heavy, intense, and often confrontational. "It took aspects of grunge, ground in some metal, and often featured rap-like vocals. It was heavy, it was intense, it was in your face, sometimes violent, sometimes misogynist, and not exactly what you'd call radio-friendly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Dominance and Polarization (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: In the late 1990s, Nu Metal became the dominant genre in rock, following the fading of earlier alt-rock movements like grunge and Britpop. This scene was highly polarizing, contributing to widespread dissatisfaction among many rock fans who felt the music being made was unappealing. "New metal ruled. And as we saw in chapter 13, that scene was very, very polarizing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Dominance in North American New Rock (Late 90s)
podcast.body: For a period, Nu Metal dominated North American new rock with its "testosterone overdose." "North American New Rock was being dominated by the testosterone overdose of new metal"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant in Late 1990s
podcast.body: New Metal was a significant genre in the late 1990s, from which bands like Linkin Park emerged, though most did not achieve the same level of enduring success. "pretty much the only group to emerge from the whole new metal thing of the late 90s bigger and stronger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence from Genre Blending
podcast.body: The intertwining of punk, funk, rap, hip hop, and metal by the end of the 1980s was identified as the precursor to the development of nu metal, which was expected to be a significant topic in future discussions of 90s alt-rock. "And who knew that in a few years would be talking about this thing called new metal?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution in Early 2000s
podcast.body: The classification of bands like Incubus in early 2000 as "new metal" prompted questions about whether the genre was evolving to become "less polarizing" or if its definition was shifting. Evanescence was also described as being on the "fringes" of new metal. "At the time, they were most generally classified as a new metal band, which was a bit odd, as a scratchy, but then, wait, was new metal evolving into something less polarizing?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Extremes of the Genre
podcast.body: Some bands, like Limp Biscuit, pushed new metal "to its extremes and beyond." "And then there were those who took new metal to its extremes and beyond. Bands like Limp Biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Industry Belief of Demise
podcast.body: By the end of 1999, record labels had turned down Linkin Park's demos almost 50 times, reflecting the music industry's belief that new metal was "over." "that's how much the industry believed that new metal was over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Queens of the Stone Age
podcast.body: The surge of new metal in the late 1990s and early 2000s, alongside the popularity of Grunge, played a role in setting the career path for Queens of the Stone Age. "with the help from the late 90s, early 2000s wave of new metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Secrets of Queens of the Stone Age: Part 2

podcast.title: Intense Metal Leanings
podcast.body: Other new metal bands, including Disturbed, Mudvayne, Lip knots, and System of a Down, were "much more intense because of their pronounced metal leanings." "Other bands were much more intense because of their pronounced metal leanings, disturbed, mud veins, lip knots, system of a down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jada Pinkett Smith's Band
podcast.body: Jada Pinkett Smith, Willow's mother, is the singer of a new metal band called Wicked Wisdom. "mom is a singer of a new metal band called Wicked Wisdom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 1990s Band Signings
podcast.body: The late 1990s saw numerous new metal bands being signed, indicating a peak in its commercial interest and label activity. "The late 1990s saw signing after signing after signing of new metal bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 1990s Popularity
podcast.body: New metal emerged as a crossover between rock and rap, becoming "insanely popular" at the end of the 1990s. For a time, it was the most popular of all alt-rock sounds despite being heavy, intense, confrontational, and sometimes featuring misogynistic and violent themes. "The result had been tagged new metal. It took aspects of grunge, ground in some metal, and often featured rap-like vocals. It was heavy, it was intense, it was in your face, sometimes violent, sometimes misogynist, and not exactly what you'd call radio-friendly. Yet for a time at the end of the 1990s, it was insanely popular."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Late 1990s Rock-Hip Hop Hybrid
podcast.body: New Metal emerged at the end of the 1990s as a significant genre that fused elements of rock and hip hop, indirectly giving rise to successful bands like Linkin Park. "then we had the whole new metal thing at the end of the 1990s which indirectly gave birth to Lincoln Park, still one of the biggest bands of the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Limp Bizkit's Impact on Nu-Metal
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit became one of the most successful and "in-your-face" bands of the new metal era following their major label deal, which was facilitated by a pivotal connection with Korn. "limp biscuit had a major label deal and were on their way to becoming one of the most successful and most in-your-face bands of the new metal era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Polarizing Form of Alt-Rock
podcast.body: New metal was characterized as "one of the most polarizing forms of alt-rock ever conceived," with some of it aging well and "the rest of it, not so much." "new metal, which was one of the most polarizing forms of alt-rock ever conceived. Some of it has aged okay. The rest of it, not so much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Polarizing Sound
podcast.body: Nu-metal emerged as a polarizing sound in the late 1990s, filling some of the void left by the decline of alternative rock. "the polarizing sound of new metal"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Popularity in Late 90s
podcast.body: This genre was prominent in the late 1990s, with bands like Limp Biscuit achieving significant sales and success. "Limp Biscuit was one of the bands of the new metal era of the late 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Eurodance Dominance (New Millennium)
podcast.body: Nu-Metal gained significant prominence on music charts and television after the decline of Eurodance. It was embraced by major channels like MTV as they shifted their programming focus away from the dance genre. "...al numital..."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La gran mentira detrás del Eurodance

podcast.title: Successor to Grunge (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: After the original grunge bands died off and the genre's popularity waned in the late 1990s, New Metal emerged as a replacement, albeit described as "Dreck-like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Woodstock 99 Lineup and Crowd Demeanor
podcast.body: The lineup for Woodstock 99 was heavily populated with "intense and angry new metal bands," including Limp Bizkit, Korn, Kid Rock, Rage Against the Machine, and Metallica. This concentration of aggressive music was cited as contributing to an atmosphere of "male rage and testosterone" among the 200,000 attendees, fostering the frustration and negative energy that escalated into widespread hatred and violence. "Added in the fact that the lineup was filled with intense and angry new metal bands, LeBiscuit corn, kid rocked, kid rocked, rage guns, the machine, Metallica, tons of mail rage and testosterone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
